Case Information: A 2-year-old female child, third in birth order, born to parents who are first cousins, delivered vaginally at term without complications, presented with sparse scalp hair, absent body hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes, and delayed tooth eruption. The mother reported that the child does not sweat and has had recurrent fevers since the neonatal period. Psychomotor development was normal. There was no family history of similar symptoms, except for a previous female sibling with similar complaints and a distinctive appearance, who experienced recurrent fever and chest infections during the neonatal period and died at 6 months of age. The parents' first pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 2 months for unknown reasons. Skin examination showed smooth, normal-looking skin with normal palmoplantar skin and dermatoglyphics. The child had an aged appearance with finely wrinkled skin around the eyes, an everted lower lip, and low-set ears. Scalp hair was sparse, light-colored, and thin, with complete absence of eyelashes, eyebrows, and body hair. Oral examination revealed only two conical, widely spaced maxillary teeth and a low-arched, flat palate. Nails were normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities, and there was no evidence of mental retardation. Imaging of the jaw showed a lack of teeth with only two maxillary teeth and a left mandibular tooth bud. Biochemical tests were normal.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathology of palmer skin from hypothenar area showed inconspicuous sweat glands.

Case Information: A 30-year-old male arrived at the emergency department experiencing shortness of breath, coughing, production of phlegm, fever, and night sweats for approximately one month. He had previously been treated with antibacterial medication at another facility for these symptoms. Although there was an initial improvement, he returned to the emergency department due to the onset of hemoptysis, which progressively worsened over the month, reaching about 300 ccs per day. A chest X-ray initially showed an enlarged right hilus.
Diagnostic Tests: CT angiography of the thorax showed bilateral pulmonary embolism at segmentary branches of pulmonary arteries and pulmonary aneurysms.

Case Information: A 4-year-old male child presented with discolored teeth. His medical history was unremarkable. The mother reported an uncomplicated, full-term pregnancy from a nonconsanguineous marriage. The child appeared well-nourished with a height of 96.25 cm. Parents noted normal mental development. The child had sparse, discolored hair and had undergone 3-4 haircuts. He had a broad forehead, prominent in lateral view, with a head circumference of 51.25 cm, within the 50th percentile. There was no splitting of the superficial layer of fingernails or toenails. Dental examination showed the eruption of all four permanent first molars. Primary teeth had been extracted due to dental abscess formation. The remaining primary teeth were opaque and yellowish-brown, with severe attrition of mandibular primary incisors and maxillary primary canines. Pulp chambers of maxillary and mandibular primary canines were visible through the thin enamel. Both posterior and anterior occlusal relationships indicated a Class III tendency. A panoramic radiograph revealed increased sclerosis of the mandibular cortical bone. The remaining primary teeth and erupted first permanent molars appeared taurodontic, with extremely thin enamel, enlarged pulp chambers with greater apico-occlusal height, and apically displaced furcation. Radiographic contrast between enamel and dentin was reduced. Root formation of the first permanent molars was incomplete, preventing an objective assessment of taurodontism. A lateral cephalogram showed increased density of the mandible, especially in the symphysis region, and the base of the skull. Frontal sinus pneumatization was not very apparent. Cephalometric analysis indicated a Class III skeletal pattern due to a retrusive maxilla (reduced SNA).
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic analysis reports of the child revealed a 4-bp mutation in the DLX3 gene.

Case Information: A 12-year-old male with no notable birth or medical history presented with concerns about lower abdominal distention and had reduced his food intake over the past 3 months. He engaged in excessive exercise relative to his food intake. Despite significant weight loss, he expressed concerns about his abdominal size. During the initial consultation, he was observed to be very lean with a body mass index (BMI) of 11.5 kg/m2 and had a heart rate of approximately 40 beats/min, indicating sinus bradycardia. Enteral nutritional supplements were administered to improve his weight. Seven days after the first visit, he was emergently hospitalized due to disorientation. On admission, his height was 145 cm, weight was 20.9 kg (BMI: 9.9 kg/m2), and he presented with impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) E3V4M6), bradycardia (heart rate ~40 beats/min), and slow breathing (respiratory rate ~10 cycles/min). Blood gas analysis and blood tests showed hypercapnia, hypoglycemia, and elevated levels of creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and transaminases. His movements were slow but not paralytic, and his cranial nerves were intact. Due to chronic hypoglycemia and dehydration, rapid correction was avoided to prevent complications such as refeeding syndrome, heart failure, pleural effusion, and ascites. Hypoglycemia and dehydration were corrected slowly (glucose infusion rate: 0.6–1.0 mg/kg/min; water: 20 mL/kg/day). On the second day of admission, he developed further impaired consciousness (GCS E1V1M1) and low blood pressure, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU). After correcting hypoglycemia and dehydration, his consciousness improved, and he was transferred to the general ward on the third day. On the fourth day, hepatic transaminases peaked with aspartate transaminase (AST) at 4,782 U/L and alanine transaminase (ALT) at 2,265 U/L, along with coagulopathy (prothrombin time (%): 28%). Liver support therapy, including glucose infusion and enteral nutrition, was provided, leading to gradual improvement in AST and ALT levels.
Diagnostic Tests: T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images showed a localized high-signal area from the cortex to the white matter of the fusiform gyrus to the parahippocampal gyrus near the left hippocampus. The cortex in high-signal lesions is thickened, the boundary between white matter and cortex is indistinct and localized, and there is no tendency for invasion into the surrounding white matter. There was no contrast enhancement.

Case Information: A 66-year-old multiparous female patient presented with recurrent vaginal bleeding and dull lower abdominal pain for 2 months. She had recently undergone vaginal sonography at a private gynecologic clinic. On admission, physical examination results were unremarkable, and her vital signs were normal. Laboratory testing indicated a CA-125 level of >1,000 U/mL (reference value, 0 to 35). A Pap smear test showed atrophy and inflammation but no evidence of malignancy.
Diagnostic Tests: EUS-guided FNB identified papillary tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and frequent mitosis. Both abdominopelvic CT and pelvic dynamic MRI revealed an 8×5×5 cm heterogeneous irregular enhancing mass, at the cul-de-sac extending to both adnexa, that had directly invaded the rectal wall. EUS revealed a sausage-shaped hypoechoic mass, 8 cm in size, with irregular margins and heterogeneous internal echoes extending to both adnexa. The solid echogenic adnexal mass had nearly obliterated the lumen of both fallopian tubes and had invaded the fundus of the uterus. Dual imaging with the conventional gray-scale B-mode EUS image and elastographic image demonstrated that the mass had a blue color pattern, representing hard stiffness, and heterogeneous green/red coloration outside the tumor, representing intermediate stiffness. The B/A strain ratio of the adnexal mass was 15.61.

Case Information: A 55-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of severe fatigue, diarrhea, and vomiting. In the emergency department, she experienced multiple apneic episodes necessitating intubation and ventilation. No infective or metabolic causes were identified. She had a history of bilateral action tremor in both upper and lower limbs for 7 months, diagnosed as benign essential tremor 2 years prior, and was on propranolol. Over the past 2 years, she lost 12 kg and was diagnosed with depression, exhibiting withdrawal and apathy. There was a family history of Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, though details were initially sparse. During her ICU stay, she had recurrent apneic episodes and worsening tremor, leading to treatment with levetiracetam and phenytoin due to jerky limb movements and a depressed conscious level. Routine blood tests were normal except for mild reversible hyponatremia. She was transferred to the ICU at a regional neurosciences center. Brain MRI was normal, and lumbar puncture showed normal cerebrospinal fluid (white cell count <1, protein 0.17 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 8.8 mmol/L, and negative oligoclonal bands). Electroencephalogram indicated encephalopathic features with continuous slow wave activity over the left frontotemporal region. She was treated with 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisolone. After respiratory weaning, she was moved to ward-level care. Her encephalopathy and apneic episodes resolved during her stay, and her mood improved significantly. Examination showed slight hypomimia, normal vertical gaze, rest tremor of the right upper and lower limbs, asymmetrical postural and action tremor worse on the right, rest tremor of the tongue, mild right-sided limb rigidity, and moderate right upper limb bradykinesia. She started on co-careldopa, and at 100/25 mg three times daily, her tremor and bradykinesia improved. Overnight oximetry revealed a desaturation index of 1.7/h, with desaturation below 85% for 12 minutes and a low of 65%, indicating sleep-disordered breathing. Immunology tests were negative for various antibodies. Further family history revealed her mother had idiopathic Parkinson's disease diagnosed at 46 and died in her early 50s, and her 57-year-old brother was being treated for rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonism with erratic breathing and had recently started on CPAP.
Diagnostic Tests: Genetic testing revealed that the patient was heterozygous for the c.211G > A, p.(G71R) pathogenic mutation in exon 2 of the DCTN1 gene.

Case Information: A 66-year-old retired male patient visited the pain clinic in mid-2014 with complaints of episodic headaches over the past 10 years. These headaches occurred up to 8 times daily, beginning as a sharp pain near the right eye and spreading to the right side of the face, vertex, and upper back of the head. Each episode lasted between 45 and 75 minutes, with pain-free intervals in between. The pain was described as intense and unbearable, accompanied by rhinorrhea in the right nostril and conjunctival injection in the right eye without swelling. The patient experienced significant restlessness during these episodes. Treatment with a greater occipital nerve block using 40 mg methylprednisolone and 20 mg bupivacaine provided complete pain relief within minutes, lasting for 12 months. This treatment was repeated twice, each time offering 6 months of relief. By mid-2016, the headaches had subsided, and the patient remained headache-free for 2.5 years. His medical history included an abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery, and his family history was unremarkable. In July 2019, the patient returned to the clinic with a new, constant stabbing pain radiating from the back of the right side of his head to the right side of the vertex, forehead, right ear, and jaw, accompanied by numbness and paresthesias. He did not report neck pain. The right eye exhibited continuous tearing, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema, along with excessive rhinorrhea. The patient felt particularly restless at night. His baseline pain score was 6 out of 10, with exacerbations reaching 9 out of 10, occurring 2-3 times daily and lasting 20-30 minutes, sometimes triggered by neck movements. Physical examination revealed mild tearing, conjunctival injection, and slight eyelid edema in the right eye, along with hyperesthesia over the right vertex and forehead. Neurological examination was otherwise normal. Passive neck extension was extremely limited and reproduced severe pain exacerbations. Palpation of the right SCM muscle elicited tenderness and exacerbated the referred pain. An injection of 30 mg of 1% lidocaine into the right SCM muscle resulted in a reduction of pain from a score of 7 out of 10 to 0 within 4 minutes. The numbness in the forehead and vertex disappeared, neck range of motion improved, and right-sided tearing and conjunctival injection began to subside, followed by resolving eyelid edema. Symptom relief lasted for 4 weeks before partially relapsing. In September 2019, the patient returned and received another injection, this time with 20 mg lidocaine and 10 mg bupivacaine, resulting in complete pain resolution for an additional 2 months.
Diagnostic Tests: The pain was relieved within 24 h of the indomethacin trial.

Case Information: A 32-year-old female presented with severe pain in the right temporomandibular joint (TMJ) region, right ear, limited mouth opening, and facial asymmetry. She was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery without perinatal or notable postnatal issues. Her parents noticed progressive enlargement of her right cheek and differing eyelid width in the months following birth. The facial asymmetry became more pronounced over the years but has remained stable recently. No other family members are affected, and her mother reported a normal pregnancy. The enlargement extended from the midline to the preauricular region and down to the lower border of the mandible. The skin on the right side of the face appeared normal with no changes in thickness. Extraoral examination showed that the right side of the mandible was larger than the left. The outer contour of the right ear was slightly larger and differently shaped compared to the left ear. The nose was normal with no deviation, but the chin was deviated toward the right side. The lower lip on the right side appeared thicker with drooping at the corner of the mouth, and the lips on the right side were very dry. The patient reported clicking in the left TMJ, difficulty chewing, and headaches on the right side. Physical examination revealed a normal symmetric body and mental health. The mouth opening was 12 mm. Intraoral examination showed tongue asymmetry with unilateral enlargement of fungiform papillae on the right side. The teeth on the affected side appeared normal except for the maxillary right first molar, which was significantly larger than the maxillary left first molar. The lower right first molar was slightly larger than the lower left first molar. The lower dental centerline was deviated to the right, and there was a downward canting of the occlusal plane. Occlusal examination revealed unattainable central relation, early contact in both central occlusion and right lateral movement, and a discrepancy in the range of mandibular motion. The patient was referred for further evaluation.
Diagnostic Tests: The radiographs confirmed the clinical findings. The panoramic radiograph showed that the right condyle, ramus, condylar neck, and the body of the mandible were enlarged. There was significant deposition of bone growth on the right mandible, and the bony trabeculation alteration was observed. The size of the right inferior dental canal was normal compared to the left mandibular canal and was displaced. Crowns and roots of the right mandibular molars were larger than the contralateral mandibular molars. The roots of the lower right first and second molars were remarkably divergent. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images of the face and skull revealed that the zygomatic and frontal bones, right mastoid process, right half of the mandible and maxilla, maxillary sinus, and associated soft tissues were enlarged. CBCT also demonstrated thickening the mucosal membrane of the right maxillary sinus. There was no obstruction in the sinus meatus. Brain computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities. 3D skull reconstruction CT image revealed hypertrophy of the right mandible, condyle, TMJ, zygomatic bone, petrous bone, and mastoid process. The posteroanterior radiograph revealed enlargement of right half of the mandible, maxilla, and zygoma.

Case Information: A 21-year-old male with no previous history of illness presented with fever, a mild headache, body aches, joint pain, and a dry cough. These symptoms started four days prior to the presentation. It was only when he noticed a rash that he came to the hospital. He had immigrated from Asia five years prior. There was no recent international travel history. He recently returned from Tennessee five days prior to the presentation. However, he reported that he did not visit the densely forested areas. On examination, there was a maculopapular, blanching rash over the volar region of the forearm, lower leg, and over his body and neck. He reported no itching or pain over the rash. He had been taking NyQuil since the onset of the fever. Despite this, his temperature was 101°F during admission. On physical examination, his conjunctiva appeared mildly injected. Besides, there was nasal congestion and a sore throat. There was diffuse muscle tenderness and arthralgia. All other systems, including the neurological, cardiovascular, and respiratory systems, were unremarkable. Measles IgM was ordered, which came back negative.
Diagnostic Tests: His complete blood count (CBC) on admission showed thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and hyponatremia.

Case Information: A 12-year-old boy from the Northwest Gondar Amhara regional state presented with left flank swelling for the past 3 months. Three days prior to admission, he began experiencing pain in the left flank, accompanied by high-grade fever, chills, rigor, and vomiting. He did not report any urinary or respiratory symptoms. His maternal pregnancy course and medical history were unremarkable, and he was born at a health center. His past medical history was also unremarkable. He has seven siblings, none of whom exhibited similar symptoms. His mother had no history of radiation exposure, use of traditional medicine, or chemotherapy during pregnancy. No dysmorphisms were observed in his general appearance. Vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 142 beats/min, respiratory rate 33 breaths/min, temperature 38.5 °C, and blood pressure 105/65 mmHg. Anthropometric measurements indicated severe stunting. Abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen, asymmetry with bulging on the left flank, a visible horizontal line, an upward umbilical slit, and absent rectus abdominis muscles. The abdomen was soft with a tender cystic mass on the left flank, measuring 13 × 11 cm, palpable bimanually. Both testes were undescended. The patient also had scoliosis and developmental dysplasia of the hips with a waddling gait. Urinary analysis showed many red blood cells and positive leukocyte esterase. Renal function tests were normal with a creatinine level of 0.72 mg/dl and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 44 mg/dl. Hemoglobin was normal at 12.7 gm/dl, and electrolyte levels were normal.
Diagnostic Tests: Ultrasound showed a large cystic mass in his left kidney area with echo debris. His right kidney had normal echo texture and size. An X-ray of his hips showed bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip. His left kidney is cystic and enlarged; there is no parenchyma tissue, both testes are intraperitoneal just below the kidneys, tortuous left renal vein, enlarged bladder reaching above umbilicus, and left megaureter.

Case Information: An 11-year-old male presented with muscle pain, weakness, lack of appetite, and vomiting. Laboratory tests showed elevated liver enzymes (AST 144 IU/L, ALT 267 IU/L) and an ultrasound revealed an enlarged liver. He is the second child in a family of three, with healthy, unrelated parents. He was born at full term with a birth weight of 3290 grams and had a normal adaptation to life outside the womb. He was breastfed until the age of 3, and his psychomotor development and growth were normal. He had episodes of asthma in early childhood. At 1 year old, he was hospitalized for elevated liver enzymes and anemia, but no further tests were conducted. He was hospitalized again at ages 4 and 5 for wheezing and asthma exacerbations. From age 6, he experienced muscle cramps without fever, easy fatigue, and muscle pain after light exercise, sometimes accompanied by vomiting. During the latest episode, tests showed decreased free carnitine and increased acylcarnitines from short to very long-chain, along with elevated levels of glutaric, 2-ketoglutaric, ethylmalonic, and dicarboxylic acids. Elevated liver enzymes (AST 90 IU/L, ALT 143 IU/L), creatine kinase (348 IU/L), and ammonia (93 μmol/L) were also noted. The plasma amino acid profile showed significant hyperprolinemia (520.1 μmol/L) and slight hyperasparaginemia (232.8 μmol/L). Neurological examination revealed preserved consciousness, general weakness, reduced muscle strength in the lower limbs, and mild muscle wasting. Heart ultrasound showed mild concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle, and liver ultrasound indicated diffuse hyperechogenicity consistent with steatosis. During hospitalization, he received intravenous glucose (10%, 4 mg/kg/min) and l-carnitine (100 mg/kg), leading to gradual clinical improvement. A trial with Rf (150 mg/day) normalized glutaric acid levels but other organic acids and acylcarnitines remained abnormal. Upon discharge, he was advised to reduce long-chain lipid intake and control protein intake in his diet. Oral l-carnitine supplementation and Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) were continued.
Diagnostic Tests: Persistent dicarboxylic aciduria and elevated ethylmalonic acid.

Case Information: A 76-year-old male with a history of hypertension managed with anti-hypertensive medication experienced a sudden, painless decrease in vision in the left eye (OS) for one day. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in the right eye (OD) and counting fingers close to face (CFCF) in the OS. A relative afferent pupillary defect was observed in the OS. Intraocular pressure was within normal limits in both eyes (OU) (OD 14 mmHg, OS 16 mmHg). The anterior segment examination was unremarkable in both eyes. Fundus examination of the OD was normal. The OS fundus examination revealed a normal-appearing optic disc with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3:1, arteriolar narrowing with segmental blood flow (box-carring), and diffuse background pallor with a small area of normal-appearing retina temporal to the optic disc, corresponding to patent cilioretinal arteries.
Diagnostic Tests: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) showed diffuse retinal thickening and inner retinal hyperreflectivity except in the small area corresponding to the patent cilioretinal arteries. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) showed an absence of flow signals in superficial, deep, and outer retinal plexuses except in a well-demarcated area nasal to the fovea. OCTA of the disc and macula OS showed the presence of three cilioretinal arteries and flow void in the rest of the vasculature.

Case Information: A twenty-four-year-old female with a lifelong history of epilepsy and cognitive impairment presented with cyclic episodes of lethargy and behavioral changes. She had a history of intrauterine toxoplasmosis infection, resulting in colpocephaly, absence of posterior hemispheric structures, bilateral parieto-occipital porencephaly, and malformation of the right frontal lobe. Partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, including an absent splenium, was also noted. Developmental delays were observed during childhood, and seizures began at age 5, with multiple seizure types including atonic and generalized tonic-clonic. Approximately two years prior to presenting to Mayo Clinic, she began experiencing episodes of hypothermia with temperatures as low as 30.5°C, systemic hypotension, lethargy, and compromised functional status, leading to hospitalization for breakthrough seizures. During these episodes, she was consistently hyponatremic. These episodes occurred monthly and resolved over one to two weeks. Over the course of two years, she was found to be thrombocytopenic, anemic, and occasionally leukopenic. These hematological changes were initially attributed to valproic acid, which was part of her antiepileptic regimen along with lamotrigine for fifteen years. Valproic acid was discontinued in January 2012, and she was switched to levetiracetam, but her blood counts continued to decline. After discontinuing levetiracetam, her seizures were managed with zonisamide, clobazam, and rufinamide, and a vagal nerve stimulator was placed. Despite these changes, her blood counts remained depressed during subsequent hospitalizations. During a recent episode of lethargy and poor responsiveness, she was admitted to her local hospital and transferred to our institution. Laboratory findings included thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 57 × 10^9/L (normal range 150–450 × 10^9/L), anemia with a hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL (12.0–15.5 g/dL) and reticulocytopenia at 12.7 × 10^9/L (38.1–112.6 × 10^9/L). Her white blood cell count was within normal limits at 6.7 × 10^9/L (3.5–10.5 × 10^9/L). An infectious workup, including HIV, parvovirus B19 PCR, and blood and urine cultures, was negative. Iron, vitamin B12, and folate levels were normal. D-dimer, fibrinogen, and coagulation studies did not indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation. The heparin-induced thrombocytopenia PF4 antibody was negative, and no rheumatoid factor was detected. Her peripheral smear was normal, and levels of arsenic, cadmium, mercury, and lead were within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: Bone marrow biopsy showed a slightly hypocellular marrow with a mild granulocytic hypoplasia and megakaryocytic hyperplasia. Trilineage maturation was within normal limits.

Case Information: The patient is a 17-year-old female presenting with proximal muscle weakness since early childhood. She is the second child of healthy, nonconsanguineous Russian parents. Her pregnancy and delivery were normal, with a birth weight of 3.80 kg and length of 52 cm. On the third day of life, she was hospitalized with pneumonia due to aspiration and required mechanical ventilation until 4.5 months old. This was her only episode of respiratory dysfunction. She experienced delayed motor development, holding her head up at 7 months, sitting at 16 months, walking at 21 months, and always needing support to stand. In early childhood, her mouth was slightly open when in a vertical position. Phrasal speech developed appropriately for her age. There was no history of seizures, and her vision and hearing were intact. At 9–10 years old, she developed a prominent scoliotic deformity of the spine, which was treated conservatively between ages 12 and 14. At 12 years old, she had surgery for ankle tendon retraction without general anesthesia. In recent years, her condition has slowly worsened, with marked gait disturbances, difficulty climbing stairs, and inability to rise from the floor independently. Her cognitive functions are normal, and she is currently studying at university. On examination, her height is 167 cm and weight is 62 kg. Phenotypic features include micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, and clinodactyly of the fifth finger of the right hand. Neurological examination revealed atrophy of the pectoral and proximal muscles, weakness in facial, neck, and limb-girdle muscles, positive Gowers’ sign, and asymmetric Trendelenburg’s gait. She also has kyphoscoliosis of the thoracic spine, lumbar hyperlordosis, and a prominent asymmetric hip position. Additionally, she has pes cavus on both sides. Leg tendon reflexes were absent, while biceps and triceps reflexes were normal. Creatine kinase levels were normal. Needle electromyography showed a myopathic pattern with no spontaneous activity.
Diagnostic Tests: The analysis revealed two heterozygous SNVs: c.862A>T, p.(Lys288Ter) and c.93del, p.(Lys32ArgfsTer78) in the STAC3 gene (ENST00000332782.7). The validation and segregation analyses of detected SNVs showed that each of the parents is a carrier of only one, which verifies the compound heterozygosity of SNVs in the proband. The healthy brother is a carrier of the heterozygous variant c.862A>T, p.(Lys288Ter).

Case Information: A 63-year-old male patient presented with a painful swelling on the inside of the right cheek, which had been increasing in size over the past month. He reported no history of jaw cysts. Clinical examination identified a firm, mobile nodule on the right buccal mucosa, just anterior to the ramus mandibulae, measuring 2.5 cm in diameter. The overlying mucosa was intact. A panoramic radiograph showed no bony lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging of the head and neck revealed an oval cystic structure in the retromolar trigone with a maximum diameter of 1.8 cm. An excision biopsy was performed.
Diagnostic Tests: Microscopy showed a cyst wall, with a parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of 5–6 cell layers in thickness, a corrugated surface and basal palisading.

Case Information: A 4-year-old boy was admitted with complaints of hard skin for over 3 years, unclear vision, and communication difficulties for one day. He was born weighing 3 kg and appeared normal at birth but soon exhibited failure to thrive. At one month old, his skin became swollen and sclerodermatous on the trunk, and he experienced loss of scalp hair and stunted growth. Prior to admission, he had blurred vision, communication difficulties, dull eyes, and an inability to speak. Physical examination revealed distinctive facial features, including prominent eyes and scalp veins, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, generalized alopecia with sparse downy hairs, a narrow nasal bridge, thin lips, micrognathia, and small ear lobes. His neck was soft, Brinell's sign was negative, Klinefelter's sign was negative, Babbitt's sign was positive bilaterally, tendon reflexes were present, limb muscle strength was grade IV, muscle tension was high, and his skin was stiff with poor elasticity and extensive mottled pigmentation on the trunk. He had bilateral metacarpophalangeal joint contracture deformity, flexion deformity of both proximal knuckles, difficulty squatting, and fixed hip and knee joint contractures, with a horse-riding posture. He measured 77 cm in height (<1st percentile) and weighed 7.8 kg (<1st percentile). He was unable to speak or communicate and was too young for a detailed ophthalmic examination. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, cardiac enzymes, serum electrolytes, and lipids, were within normal limits. Electrocardiogram and ultrasonic cardiogram showed no anomalies. Radiographic examination indicated general osteoporotic changes, short and dystrophic clavicles, and distal phalanges osteolysis. Lateral skull X-ray showed cranial dysplasia, and chest X-ray revealed bilateral clavicle dysplasia and rib deformity. Carotid artery B-ultrasound showed 0.05 cm intima-media thickening in both common carotid arteries. EEG indicated moderate abnormalities with irregular delta waves. Brain MRI showed multiple abnormal signals in the bilateral frontoparietal cortex, bilateral semiovale center, and lateral ventricle, as well as in the deep frontoparietal white matter, suggesting cerebral infarction. Cranial MRA revealed bilateral internal carotid artery stenosis with basilar artery and thickening of the bilateral posterior communicating artery. A follow-up head MRI after 3 months showed bilateral paraventricular and central semiovale lacunar infarction. A follow-up head MRA after 3 months showed similar findings to the previous one.
Diagnostic Tests: The patient carried a c.1824C > T (p.G608G) heterozygous LMNA mutation.

Case Information: A 13-year-old male was admitted due to progressive difficulty in walking and clumsiness, first noticed by his mother around the age of 5. His birth history and early neurodevelopment until 1 year of age were normal. He achieved head control at 3 months, rolled over at 5 months, and sat independently at 10 months. Subsequent developmental milestones were delayed: standing with support at 16 months and walking independently at 21 months. He spoke his first meaningful words at 2 years, formed phrases at 4 years, and constructed simple sentences by 5 years. At 5 years old, his mother observed a slow, broad-based gait and generalized weakness in his movements, but no medical consultation was sought at that time. His walking difficulties gradually worsened, and he recently experienced challenges in academic performance. The patient has one sister. His father died in a car accident at age 40. There is no family history of neurological disorders or renal stones. On admission, physical examination revealed minor dysmorphic features, including a long face, macrognathia, high arched palate, and large ears. Neurological examination showed mild higher cortical dysfunction, dysarthria, upper limb and gait ataxia, hyperreflexia with bilateral extensor toe signs. Motor power and muscle tone were normal. Sensory examination was normal except for impaired vibration and position sense in the lower extremities. Cranial nerve functions were intact, and optic fundi appeared normal. There were no tremors or involuntary movements. Neuropsychological evaluation indicated mild mental retardation with a full-scale intelligence quotient of 62, a verbal scale intelligence quotient of 79, and a performance scale intelligence quotient of 47. Somatosensory evoked potential testing of the posterior tibial nerve showed no cortical waves (P1), indicating central conduction dysfunction through the posterior column of the spinal cord. However, spine MRI did not reveal any structural lesions in the spinal cord. Electromyography, nerve conduction study, and brain MRI were normal. Chromosome analysis and Fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene studies were normal. Routine urinalysis and abdominal ultrasonography showed no evidence of urolithiasis. Cerebrospinal fluid examination, serum and cerebrospinal fluid lactate/pyruvate levels, urine organic acid analysis, and plasma amino acid analysis were normal.
Diagnostic Tests: Quantitative amino acid analysis of the urine disclosed increased excretion of cystine (1,345 µM/g Cr) and an excess of the dibasic amino acids; ornithine, lysine, and arginine. The oral cystine loading test resulted in elevation of plasma cystine levels. Direct sequencing of entire coding region of SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 genes of the patient revealed both a G (normal) and A (mutant) at nucleotide 535 in exon 5, resulting in the presence of a Gly (codon GGA) at amino acid position 173 and a Arg (codon AGA) in heterozygote state.

Case Information: A 30-year-old Jamaican-American male presented with one month of bilateral foot pain and ulcerations, with severe pain on the bottom of his left foot. He was active-duty military and a former professional athlete with no significant past medical history. He reported numbness on the plantar surface of both feet, which progressed to pain, worse at night and unrelieved by compression and over-the-counter pain medications. Physical examination revealed intact vibratory sensation in the lower extremities, extreme tenderness to palpation on the left foot, decreased dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of both feet, and decreased sensation on the plantar surface of the left foot. After a trial of compression stockings, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen, he presented to the emergency department with worsening foot pain. D-dimer was elevated, and bilateral lower extremity ultrasound was negative for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). He was referred to a vascular clinic, where he had a normal ankle-brachial index of 0.96 on the right and 0.98 on the left. He was then referred to dermatology and neurology for further evaluation. Dermatology started him on a topical steroid cream. At the neurology evaluation, his pain had significantly worsened, and he required a wheelchair due to inability to ambulate. There was no improvement in pain or skin lesions despite the prescribed treatments. Electromyography (EMG) showed severe diffuse axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy affecting the bilateral lower extremities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed mild degenerative disc disease with mild bilateral neural foraminal narrowing at L5-S1 and no significant spinal canal narrowing. Neurology referred him to rheumatology, hematology, and a second dermatologist. Laboratory evaluation showed elevated C3 and C4 complement levels at 177 mg/dL (82-167 mg/dL) and 51 mg/dL (12-38 mg/dL), respectively. Complement CH50 was elevated at >60 U/mL (>41 U/mL). Anti-nuclear antibody test was positive at a 1:160 ratio in a speckled pattern. Cardiolipin antibody IgM was elevated at 22 MPL/mL (0-12 MPL/mL). Other tests, including HIV, hepatitis A/B/C panel, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) panel, serum protein electrophoresis, kappa and lambda free light chains panel, and serum electrolytes, were negative.
Diagnostic Tests: Ulcerated epidermis with neutrophilic abscess, small vessels with fibroid necrosis of the vessel wall, and pigment-laden macrophages. No evidence of a fungal infection. Perivascular inflammation with inflammatory cells within the vessel walls. Intravascular thrombosis and eosinophilic fibrinous exudate within the vessel walls. Overlying, nonulcerated, epidermis is relatively unremarkable and uninvolved. Vessels away from the ulcer demonstrated intravascular thrombosis with some eosinophilic exudate within the vascular walls. Neovascularization noted. No intravascular hyaline deposits. Extensive hemosiderin noted on the iron stain. CD31 and ERG immunohistochemistry highlighted vascular endothelium. Immunofluorescence showed IgM in the superficial, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. C3 was 2+ clumps in the superficial, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. Fibrinogen was 2+ in the superficial walls, mid-dermal, and deep dermal blood vessels. IgG, IgG4, and IgA were all negative.

Case Information: A 14-year-old male presented with a 5-year history of a non-painful, protruding mass located in the right preauricular area. Physical examination identified a firm, dome-shaped mass measuring 1.5 cm in diameter, which was attached to the overlying skin but did not cause any skin changes. The entire mass was excised under local anesthesia. Upon gross examination, the mass appeared reddish-brown, globular, and had a stony hard consistency.
Diagnostic Tests: Microscopic examination showed a well-circumscribed nodular tumor with florid osseous metaplasia. The tumor was mainly comprised of shadow cell clusters and laminated trabecular bones with no basaloid components. The stroma admixed with shadow cell clusters showed extensive ossification along with osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. Bone marrow structures containing a few mononuclear cells and fibrofatty tissue were observed enclosed by bony trabeculae. On immunohistochemistry, these marrow cells were positive for antimyeloperoxidase antibodies.

Case Information: A 22-year-old male from Nepal experienced intermittent nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and breathlessness over the past two months. These symptoms worsened in the last 10 days, accompanied by facial puffiness, pedal edema, decreased urine output, and continued breathlessness. He reported no orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, seizures, hematuria, pyuria, or lithuria. There was no family history of similar conditions. Ten years ago, he sustained a spinal fracture from a fall, which was treated with open reduction and internal fixation. Physical examination showed a pulse rate of 86 beats per minute and blood pressure of 140/80 mm Hg. He appeared pale with an elevated jugular venous pressure of approximately 7 cm. Bilateral pitting pedal edema was noted. Nail deformities were observed in all fingers and toes, particularly in the thumbs. He also had deformed knee joints and fixed flexion deformity of both hip joints. Chest examination revealed fine crepitations in the basal regions. Cardiovascular examination indicated normal heart sounds with a functional systolic murmur in the pulmonary area, without pericardial rub. Abdominal and central nervous system examinations were normal. Fundus examination showed grade II hypertensive retinopathy. Laboratory results indicated renal impairment with urea at 20 mg% and creatinine at 28%. Initial arterial blood gas analysis revealed metabolic acidosis. A 24-hour urine protein test showed nephrotic range proteinuria (3 g/day) without active sediments in the routine urine examination. Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder revealed a right kidney measuring 9.9 cm with an ill-defined corticomedullary junction and a non-visualized left kidney, suggesting it might be ectopic or absent.
Diagnostic Tests: X-Ray of B/L knee joint showed dysplastic patellae. X-Ray of the pelvis showed B/L iliac horn. A computerised tomogram of B/L kidneys revealed the presence of both shrunken left and right kidneys (7 cm each).
